summary: Desert animals (ages 7-9): how animals survive where water is scarce and temperatures swing. The defining desert challenge is DRYNESS, not just heat. Learners separate two problems — staying cool AND keeping water in — and sort adaptations (nocturnality, burrowing, water from food, large thin ears, pale/waxy skin) under the problem each solves. Core corrections: deserts are defined by low rainfall (cold deserts like the Gobi and Antarctica exist); camel humps store FAT not water; deserts are full of life mostly hidden by day.
misconceptions: 'All deserts are hot' — a desert is defined by very low rainfall; cold deserts (Gobi, Antarctic) exist.
'Camels store water in their humps' — humps store fat, not water; water is conserved through many other adaptations.
'Deserts are empty/dead' — they are full of life that is mostly hidden by day and active at night.
'Every animal needs to drink water' — some desert animals get nearly all their water from their food.
'Big ears are just for hearing' — in desert mammals large thin ears also radiate body heat to keep cool.

activities.title: Survive the desert day: a 24-hour resource balance
steps: In a simplified hot-desert kangaroo-rat model, schedule when this seed-eating animal is active or rests in its burrow. Choose its food and observe the model’s temperature and water consequences; do not generalise this diet or schedule to every desert animal.
Watch two consequences respond to your choices: a body-temperature meter and a body-water meter.

Try activity at high noon on open sand and observe the temperature meter spike while water drains fast; then send the animal underground and schedule foraging for the cool night and observe both settle into a safe range.
Feed the animal seeds and watch the water meter refill without the animal ever finding a puddle — the water comes from the food as the body breaks it down.

Compare a separately labelled cold-desert scenario: dryness remains a challenge, but check which times and shelters suit the represented animal’s temperature needs. Do not assume the hot-desert animal’s night schedule works unchanged in freezing conditions.
activities.insight: For the represented hot-desert kangaroo rat, avoiding midday heat and using a burrow can reduce heat and water stress, and food metabolism supplies water. Other desert animals use different diets and schedules. Deserts are dry, but their temperatures and animal adaptations vary.

activities.title: Explore a desert scene by day and by night
steps: View a desert scene and toggle between midday (bare, shimmering sand) and night (active foragers emerge).

Tap each animal (camel, fennec fox, kangaroo rat, meerkat, desert tortoise, scorpion, rattlesnake) to reveal its coping strategy; label the scene as a mix of animals from different deserts around the world, not one real place.
Follow a 'where's the water?' trail from an animal to its food source, such as seeds, to see where its water comes from.
activities.insight: A hot-desert scene can reveal nocturnal species hidden during the day. Each represented animal has its own activity pattern and heat/water strategies; some desert animals are active by day, so use species-specific information.

activities.title: Sort adaptations and compare extremities
steps: Match each adaptation to the problem it solves: 'staying cool' or 'keeping water in' (some solve both).
Sort animals by when they are usually active (day, night, or it varies, e.g. by season or at dawn and dusk) and by habitat (hot desert vs cold desert).
Compare a fennec fox's huge thin ears with an Arctic fox's tiny ears, and explain how the same body part is tuned to shed heat in the desert but conserve it in the cold.
Answer targeted questions that confront common errors, e.g. 'What is really inside a camel's hump?' and 'Can a freezing place be a desert?'
activities.insight: Adaptations map onto two distinct survival problems, and the SAME trade-off (ear size shedding vs conserving heat) can solve opposite problems in opposite habitats. A desert is defined by dryness, and the camel's hump stores fat, not water.

activities.title: Optional hook: ask a desert ecologist
steps: Pose questions to an in-role desert ecologist, such as 'How does anything live out here?' or 'Where do animals find water?'
Use the answers to generate predictions to test in the balance activity.
activities.insight: Curiosity about survival in a harsh place motivates investigating the mechanisms of heat avoidance and water conservation.

checkQuestion: Everyone knows a camel can go a long time without drinking in the desert. Some children think its hump is full of water. What do you think is really inside the hump, and how does it help the camel survive?
checkAnswer: The hump stores FAT, not water. The fat is an energy reserve the camel lives off when food and water are scarce (and breaking down the fat also releases a little water). This, plus drinking huge amounts when water is available and losing little water day-to-day, is how the camel survives long dry stretches.
